newsitem.title: JAPAN: E.Asian Grain - Japan to take lead from USDA report.
newsitem.headline: E.Asian Grain - Japan to take lead from USDA report.

text.p: Japanese buyers will take their cue from the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) crop coming out later in the week in their quest to find the right time to re-enter the international market, traders said on Monday.

"We're trying to catch up with what happened during the New Year holidays. I think Japanese buyers will keep a low profile throughout this week," a corn trader said. "The USDA's crop report will be a factor."
The USDA report is due out on Thursday, January 9.
Japanese premiums for U.S. corn were quoted at nearly 100 U.S. cents a bushel over the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) May contract, traders said.
Some Japanese trade houses were negotiating with Argentina on possible corn import contracts for 1997, they said.
"But, unlike last year, there's no supply tightness in the market at the moment and no urgency to buy grain," another grains trader said.
Soybean traders said they would be sidelined this week.
Japan's Food Agency said it would carry out an import tender for 60,000 tonnes of rice on January 9.
The freight cost from the U.S. Gulf to Japan for bulk grains was seen at about US$26.50 a tonne.

While Japan awaits the USDA report, buyers in Taiwan, the Philippines and South Korea were mulling possible purchases over the next two weeks to take advantage of softer futures prices in the United States, the traders said.
Taiwan is expected to tender for up to 124,000 tonnes of U.S. corn and 38,000 tonnes of soybeans, dealers said.

South Korea's Daehan has invited tenders to buy 21,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat for March 5-April 5 shipment and the country's National Livestock Cooperatives Federation (NLCF) is also tendering for 105,000 tonnes of feed wheat on Tuesday.
An official with a local soybean processor in South Korea said his company would check for price quotations for up to 15,000 tonnes of U.S. soybeans for February shipment this week.
But most South Korean corn buyers will probably not move into the market until the USDA releases the January crop report this week, traders said.
"We expect Korean buyers to continue holding back their grain purchases until the USDA's January report," said a trader with the NLCF.
Some South Korean traders were also watching the offer price of Chinese corn which is currently quoted at around US$137 to $140 a tonne C&F, the NLCF trader said.

"The Chinese corn price has been falling to around $137 to $140 a tonne on a cost and freight basis so far. If it is $5 a tonne lower than the U.S. corn price, there will be some buying interest by local traders," the NLCF trader said.

U.S. corn is currently quoted at about $142 C&F South Korea. He said the freight rate from the Pacific Northwest remained firm at $14 to $14.50 a tonne and the rate from the U.S. Gulf at $24.00-$24.50 a tonne.
Freight rates for spot shipments were seen hovering at $16 a tonne from the U.S. Pacific Northwest and at $26 a tonne from the U.S. Gulf.
In Taiwan, the Members Feed Industry Group may place a tender for at least one 54,000-tonne corn shipment within the next two weeks.
"U.S. corn prices are nearing bottom," a buyer with the Group said.
The price of the March corn contract on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) ended two U.S. cents down at $2.56-1/2 a bushel on Friday.
Philippine firms were also thinking of buying U.S. wheat but have not made up their minds as to the size of the purchases, traders said.
